syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

concepts.learning_objective: Describe mathematics as the search for patterns and for explanations of why they exist.
Explain why finding the reason behind a pattern matters and how it leads to applications.
Identify number theory as the branch of mathematics that studies patterns in whole numbers.
Recognise the rule of each key number sequence and extend it.
Form Virahanka numbers by adding the two previous terms.
Explain sequence names such as triangular, square and cube numbers using dot and block pictures.
Recognise hexagonal numbers and find further terms.
Show that one number can be arranged in more than one pictorial shape.
Show that adding consecutive odd numbers from 1 gives square numbers and use this to find sums.
Use the pattern of adding counting numbers up and then down to obtain square numbers.
Find and use other relations among sequences, such as sums of triangular numbers and powers of 2.
Identify geometry as the branch that studies patterns in shapes in one, two or three dimensions.
Recognise the rule of shape sequences such as regular polygons, stacked squares and the Koch snowflake.
Relate the sides and corners of regular polygons to the counting numbers from 3, and explain the meaning of 'regular'.
Relate the number of lines in complete graphs to the triangular numbers.
Count little squares, little triangles and Koch snowflake segments and name the number sequences they form.
Describe a point as a precise location with no length, breadth or height.
Identify a line segment as the shortest path between two end points and name it.
Recognise that a line extends endlessly both ways and that two points determine a unique line.
Describe a ray as a part of a line with one starting point going endlessly in one direction.
Name a ray correctly using its starting point first and any other point on it.
Identify the vertex and arms of an angle formed by two rays with a common starting point.
Name angles using three letters with the vertex as the middle letter.
Explain the size of an angle as the amount of turn about the vertex.
Compare two angles by superimposing them with their vertices overlapping.
Compare angles without superimposition using a transparent circle centred at the vertex.
Recognise that the size of an angle does not depend on the lengths of its arms.
Relate straight and right angles to half and quarter turns.
Identify perpendicular lines as lines meeting at right angles and justify right angles made by folding.
Classify angles as acute or obtuse by comparing them with a right angle.
Use the fact that a full turn is 360 degrees to find measures of angles.
Read and draw angles correctly with a protractor.
Explain bisecting an angle and find angles made by repeated halving.

topics.title: Types of angles and their measures

concepts.learning_objective: Classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex from their degree measures.
Find the measure of a reflex angle from the angle on the other side.
Find an unknown angle using the fact that a straight angle measures 180 degrees.

topics.title: Numbers can tell us things and supercells

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret numbers that tell how many taller neighbours each child in a line has.
Identify supercells as cells whose number is greater than all adjacent cells and reason about them.

topics.title: Number line and playing with digits

concepts.learning_objective: Read and place large numbers at evenly spaced marks on a number line.
Count how many numbers have a given number of digits and how often a digit occurs.
Find digit sums and build numbers with a given digit sum.
Recognise and form palindromes that read the same from left to right and right to left.
Apply the reverse-and-add procedure until a palindrome is reached.

topics.title: Kaprekar's magic number, clock and calendar numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Carry out Kaprekar's largest-minus-smallest steps and recognise 6174 and 495.
Find palindromic and patterned times on a 12-hour clock.
Make a target number mentally by adding and subtracting given numbers.
Decide how many digits a sum or difference of numbers of given sizes can have.

topics.title: Number patterns and the Collatz conjecture

concepts.learning_objective: Find the sum of numbers arranged in a pattern using grouping or multiplication.
Form Collatz sequences and explain why the conjecture is still unsolved.
Make reasonable estimates of quantities when an exact count is not needed.
Judge whether a stated estimate is reasonable using rough calculation.
Follow the rules of number games such as the game of 21.
Find the key numbers that give a winning strategy in a counting game.

topics.title: What is data and why we collect it

concepts.learning_objective: Define data as a collection of facts, numbers, measures or observations that convey information.
Decide when a question needs data to be collected and use collected data to answer it.

topics.title: Organising data: tally marks and frequency tables

concepts.learning_objective: Record and read counts using tally marks grouped in fives.
Prepare and interpret a frequency table, including totals found from it.
Arrange raw data in ascending order to find the largest, smallest and counts of values.
Read a pictograph, including half symbols, to find and compare frequencies.
Choose and use a suitable scale or key so that each symbol stands for one or many units.
Read the value shown by each bar and compare categories in a bar graph.
Use the scale of a bar graph to convert bar lengths to values and draw inferences.
State the rules for drawing a bar graph: equal widths, equal gaps and markings starting from zero.
Calculate the height of each bar by dividing the value by the chosen scale.
Choose a scale for a bar graph that fits the space and suits the smallest and largest values.
Choose vertical bars (column graphs) or horizontal bars to suit the kind of quantity shown.
Evaluate whether an infographic presents data accurately or could mislead its audience.
Find common multiples of two numbers using the idli-vada game and the smallest number divisible by several numbers.
Find common factors of two or more numbers and relate them to jump sizes that reach every treasure.
Classify numbers as prime, composite or neither by counting their factors.
Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes to list the prime numbers up to 100 and explain why it works.
Identify co-prime pairs as numbers with no common factor other than 1, using the safe-treasure game.
Relate the first common multiple of two numbers to their product when the numbers are co-prime.
Write a number greater than 1 as a product of primes and recognise that this factorisation is unique apart from order.
Find the prime factorisation of a product by combining the prime factorisations of its factors.

topics.title: Using prime factorisation for co-primes and divisibility

concepts.learning_objective: Decide whether two numbers are co-prime by looking for a common prime factor in their prime factorisations.
Decide whether one number divides another by checking if its prime factorisation is included in the other's.
Use the last digit of a number to test divisibility by 2, 5 and 10 and to find remainders.
Use the number formed by the last two or three digits to test divisibility by 4 and by 8.

topics.title: Fun with numbers: special numbers and prime puzzles

concepts.learning_objective: Give reasons why a number in a group is special, using properties such as prime, composite, even, odd and square.
Solve grid puzzles in which prime numbers must give the stated row and column products.

topics.title: Perimeter of rectangles, squares and triangles

concepts.learning_objective: State that the perimeter of a closed figure is the total length of its boundary, the sum of all sides for a polygon.
Use the formulas 2 x (length + breadth) and 4 x side to find the perimeter of rectangles and squares.
Find an unknown side length when the perimeter and the other sides of a figure are known.
Apply perimeter to fencing, lace, rope and cost problems.
Find and compare distances covered in several rounds of a rectangular or square track.
Identify regular polygons and find their perimeter as number of sides x length of a side.
Explain why a diagonal of a grid square is longer than a side when finding perimeters on a grid.
Reason how the perimeter changes when pieces of a shape are joined in different ways.
Describe area as the region enclosed by a closed figure, measured in square units.
Use length x width and side x side to find areas and missing dimensions.
Find the area of a region left over after parts of it are covered or removed.
Estimate the area of a shape on squared paper using the counting conventions for full, more than half, half and less than half squares.
Explain why squares are the preferred unit shape for measuring area.
Compare the areas of tangram pieces and reason that rearranging pieces keeps the total area unchanged.
Show that a triangle drawn on the side of a rectangle with its third vertex on the opposite side has half the area of the rectangle.
Find the area of a figure by splitting it into rectangles and triangles.
Recognise that figures with the same area can have different perimeters, and the reverse.
Solve puzzles and plans that combine area and perimeter reasoning.
Express the share each person gets when a whole number of things is shared equally as a fraction.
Compare fractional units by reasoning that sharing among more people gives a smaller share.

topics.title: Fractional Units as Parts of a Whole and Measuring

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the fractional unit obtained when a whole is divided into equal parts, whatever their shape.
Describe a fractional quantity as a number of fractional units and read a fraction such as 3/4 as '3 times 1/4'.

topics.title: Marking Fraction Lengths on the Number Line

concepts.learning_objective: Find and mark fraction lengths on the number line by dividing a unit into equal parts.
Recognise that there are endlessly many fractions between 0 and 1 and locate fractions between given values.
Find the whole units in a fraction greater than 1 and write it as a mixed number.
Convert a mixed number into a fraction by counting its fractional units.
Recognise and generate equivalent fractions using the fraction wall and equal-share situations.
Express a fraction in lowest terms by dividing the numerator and denominator by common factors.
Compare fractions by converting them to equivalent fractions with a common denominator.
Compare fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about shares.
Add fractions with the same or different denominators using Brahmagupta's method.
Subtract fractions with the same or different denominators using Brahmagupta's method.

topics.title: A Pinch of History and Unit Fraction Puzzles

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how fractions were named, written and worked with in ancient India and how the notation spread.
Reason about writing fractions and the number 1 as sums of different fractional units.

topics.title: Circles and the compass in artwork

concepts.learning_objective: Describe a circle as all points at the same distance (radius) from its centre.
Use a compass with a fixed radius to draw circles and half circles in artwork such as the wavy wave.

topics.title: Squares and rectangles: properties and names

concepts.learning_objective: State the two defining properties of a rectangle and of a square.
Name a rectangle or square by listing its corners in an order of travel around it.
Explain why a rotated square or rectangle keeps its properties, including on a dot grid.
Construct a square of given side using a ruler, perpendiculars and a compass.
Construct a rectangle of given sides and check that it satisfies the rectangle properties.
Investigate how the distance between points moving on opposite sides of a rectangle changes.
Plan with a rough diagram and construct rectangles that divide into identical squares.
Use side lengths to place a square inside a rectangle with the same centre.
Compare the diagonals of a rectangle and the angles into which a diagonal divides its corners.
Construct a rectangle when a diagonal divides its opposite angles into given parts.
Construct a rectangle from one side and a diagonal using an arc to locate a corner.

topics.title: Points equidistant from two given points

concepts.learning_objective: Locate a point at given distances from two points by drawing intersecting arcs.
Plan the order of steps in a construction such as the House figure.
Construct a 4-sided figure with all sides equal that is not a square.

topics.title: Symmetry in the world around us

concepts.learning_objective: Describe symmetry as parts of a figure that repeat in a definite pattern.
Distinguish symmetrical figures such as a rangoli or butterfly from figures with no repeating pattern such as clouds.

topics.title: Line of symmetry and figures with more than one line of symmetry

concepts.learning_objective: Define a line of symmetry as a line along which a figure folds into two exactly overlapping parts.
Find the number of lines of symmetry of squares, rectangles and triangles of different kinds.
Explain that a figure with a line of symmetry has reflection symmetry, each side being reflected onto the other.
Track where the labelled corners of a square go when it is reflected in a line of symmetry.

topics.title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise that the fold is the line of symmetry of ink blot, cut-out and punched designs.
Predict the holes and shapes obtained when folded paper is punched or cut and then unfolded.

topics.title: Rotational symmetry and angles of symmetry

concepts.learning_objective: Define the centre of rotation, an angle of symmetry and when a figure has rotational symmetry.
List the angles of symmetry of figures such as a square and a paper windmill.

topics.title: Rotational symmetry of figures with radial arms

concepts.learning_objective: Find the angle between equally spaced radial arms as 360 degrees divided by the number of arms.
Use the facts that angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest one and that a whole-number smallest angle is a factor of 360.

topics.title: Symmetries of a circle and figures with both kinds of symmetry

concepts.learning_objective: State that every angle is an angle of symmetry of a circle and every diameter is a line of symmetry.
Classify figures as having reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry, both or neither.

topics.title: Bela's Building of Fun: positive and negative numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Use positive and negative numbers to name floors above and below a reference level, and recognise that zero is neither positive nor negative.
Interpret addition of integers as Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor and as combining button presses.
Find the inverse of an integer and use it to return to zero.
Compare and order integers using floors and the symbols < and >.
Interpret subtraction of integers as Target Floor - Starting Floor = Movement needed, including with larger numbers in a mine.
Recognise that subtracting a negative number is the same as adding the corresponding positive number.

topics.title: The number line and the unmarked number line

concepts.learning_objective: Place integers on the number line and describe movements along it.
Use an unmarked number line to add and subtract larger integers.
Convert a subtraction into addition of the inverse, and vice versa.
Add integers with positive and negative tokens by removing zero pairs.
Subtract integers with tokens, adding zero pairs when there are not enough tokens to take away.
Represent credits as positive and debits as negative numbers and find a bank balance.
Use integers for heights relative to sea level and for temperatures above and below 0 degrees Celsius.
Find and complete border sums in hollow integer grids.
Decide whether sums and differences of positive and negative integers are positive, negative or either.
Solve puzzles with integers such as listing integers between two numbers and possible dice sums.
Describe the early use of negative numbers in China and India and their later acceptance elsewhere.
Apply Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction of positive numbers, negative numbers and zero.
